title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days, after working through the topics and taking your mocks. The aim is to sharpen what you know, not learn new material. Most days take about an hour; the day after the full mock takes up to 90 minutes, and mock days longer.
how_it_works: Short reviews spread over several days hold up better than one long session the night before.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Time follows the exam weights, so Risk Response and Reporting, nearly a third of the exam, gets the most this week.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with today's plan. Doubling up turns review into cramming.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock, ideally at the time of day your exam starts, to test your pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Take a full timed mock in one sitting, at your exam's start time if you can, with your phone away and no notes.
Aim for about 90 seconds a question. Past 2 minutes, pick your best answer, flag it and move on. Take any break at the 2-hour checkpoint; the clock runs on.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: One mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. A practice score is not an ISACA scaled score and cannot predict your result.

days.title: Learn from your misses
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to its thinking slip, then recall the two heaviest domains. Stop at about 90 minutes; leftover misses return on day 3.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from your latest mock, newest first.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list three Domain 3 and three Domain 1 points. Then open the lists and check.
Read the principles on your role: who owns the risk, who decides the response and who answers for each control.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: Know the risk, close a gap
days.goal: Recall how risk is rated, then work on the domain where your readiness is furthest behind its weight on the exam.

tasks.text: Without looking, define inherent, current, residual and target risk, and say which one you compare with appetite. Then open the Domain 2 list and check.
Answer a short set in your focus domain, rating how sure you are before you check each answer.
Review first the answers you felt sure of but got wrong. Those are the ones to fix.
For a topic you missed more than once, read its note, then close it and explain the idea in two sentences.
Read the principles on knowing the risk before anyone acts on it.

days.remember: Current risk counts only controls in place and shown to work. A planned control changes target risk, not current risk.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your exam pace sharp with one timed mini mock, and recall how responses are chosen, tracked and reported.

tasks.text: Take a timed mini mock in one sitting. Watch the pace checks more than the score.
Without looking, name the four risk responses, who chooses among them and when acceptance fits. Then check the principles on choosing the response.
From memory, say what makes a good key risk indicator (KRI) and where its thresholds come from. Then check the note.
Read the principles on watching and reporting, including who hears about a tolerance breach.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Technology through a risk lens
days.goal: Recall Domain 4 as risk decisions, not technical how-to, sharpen how you read questions and work on your second gap.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Domain 4 points and who decides each one (risk owner, data owner, senior management or incident lead). Then open the list and check.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short set in your second-weakest domain. Name the priority word before you read the options.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: A new tool or AI system is neither banned nor adopted on faith. It is owned, assessed against appetite, then decided.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Recall everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details, so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each domain, recall two points before you open its list, starting with Domain 3. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Read the principles on what matters most: business objectives, appetite and tolerance.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your booking, ID and route, or run the online system check again.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: say the answering steps and your pace plan from memory, then check them. Stop after 15 minutes.
Read the one-line rule for your most common slip on the principles list.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your booking is confirmed, and you have checked the ID and exam-day rules in ISACA's current candidate guide.
Online: the system check is done and your desk is clear. Test center: your route and travel time are planned.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your pace plan: about 90 seconds a question, reaching questions 40, 80 and 120 at the 1-, 2- and 3-hour marks.
Arrive at least 30 minutes early, or start online check-in when it opens.
Remind yourself of your role: you identify, analyze, recommend, monitor and report, and the business owns the risk.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, flag the question and come back to it.

points.text: Roles: the board and senior management set appetite and tolerance; senior management assigns risk owners; the risk owner accepts risk and decides the response; you, the risk practitioner, identify, analyze, recommend, facilitate, monitor and report.
Each risk has one named business owner: the manager accountable for the objective at stake, never IT, the CISO, a vendor or a committee. Where nobody owns a risk, establishing ownership comes first.

Capacity is the most loss the enterprise can survive; appetite is the broad amount of risk it accepts, inside capacity; tolerance is the acceptable variation around appetite for a specific risk, often a measurable limit. No tolerance may reach capacity.
A validated tolerance breach is a governance event. Escalate it promptly to the risk owner and the level that set the limit; never accept it quietly, raise the limit or hold it for the next report.
Three lines: the first line owns and runs risks and controls; the second line, where you usually sit, oversees and challenges; the third line, internal audit, gives independent assurance.
IT risk is business risk: it sits in the enterprise register on one shared taxonomy and scale. You draft and maintain the risk framework; senior management approves it and the board oversees it.
Compliance is a minimum, not proof of low risk. Treat each obligation as a risk source with an owner, and still assess risks no rule covers. Outsourcing moves the work, never the accountability.
Risk is likelihood and business impact together, over a stated time frame. A vulnerability's severity score or a business impact analysis (BIA) ranking is one input, never the risk rating itself.

A usable risk scenario names the actor, the event, the asset, the timing and the business consequence. Build it top-down from objectives, check it bottom-up from threats, and have business owners validate it.

Inherent risk is before controls; current risk is today's exposure; residual risk is what an implemented response leaves; target risk, the future residual risk, is where a planned response should bring it.
Compare current risk, not inherent risk, with appetite. A planned or approved control changes the target, not today's rating, until evidence shows it is in place and working.

The BIA measures impact over time, not likelihood, and business owners supply it. The recovery time objective (RTO) must fit inside the maximum tolerable outage (MTO); the recovery point objective (RPO) sets tolerable data loss.
Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) is single loss expectancy times annual rate of occurrence. A control is justified on cost when it costs no more each year than the loss it avoids.
A closed incident is not a closed risk. Link loss events, near misses and AI bias or drift to their scenario, reassess likelihood and impact, and let the risk owner decide any change.

Compare risk with appetite. Within it, the owner accepts and monitors; above it, the owner mitigates, transfers or avoids, or escalates to the level that set the limit. You lay out options with cost and target risk; the owner chooses.
The best response brings risk within appetite at a cost no greater than the loss it avoids. The strongest control loses to a cheaper one that meets appetite.

Acceptance is written, by a risk owner with authority for that level. Exceptions need the risk owner's approval, compensating controls and an expiry. You assess, document and monitor; you never accept risk or grant exceptions.

The risk owner is accountable for the risk; the control owner is accountable for the control being implemented and operating effectively. Transfer and outsourcing shift cost or work, never accountability.

Implementation is not completion. Close an action plan only on evidence that the control works and the risk reached its target, or when the risk owner records a new decision. Statements and status colors are not evidence.

Key risk indicators (KRIs) track exposure, key control indicators control health and key performance indicators performance. Prefer a few leading KRIs tied to top scenarios, with thresholds from tolerance and an owner who acts.
Report to the level that can decide, in its terms, with trend and thresholds. Validate the data first, never average heat-map scores, and escalate a confirmed breach now, not at the next report.

New or off-roadmap technology, AI included, is neither banned nor adopted on faith. Record it with a proposed business owner, assess it against appetite and recommend conditions; senior management decides on adoption.
A model change is a change: retraining, new data or a new version needs validation, business-owner approval and a rollback plan, then monitoring for drift and bias like any other risk.

Set control requirements at the earliest phase of the system development life cycle (SDLC). Before launch, the risk owner accepts residual risk within appetite or asks for more treatment; developers and you never accept it.

Fast incident closure is not risk reduction. Repeat incidents call for problem management to find the root cause, with the fix through change control. Growing emergency changes are a risk signal to report.
The data owner decides classification, access and retention; IT, as custodian, carries them out. Privacy is not security: check purpose and lawful use before personal data moves, including into AI.
A backup or recovery plan counts only once restored or tested. In a declared ransomware incident, contain first, verify the backup is clean, then restore; the incident lead and business owner decide.
No single control is enough for a critical asset: look for layers, least privilege and separated duties. Certification or framework alignment is evidence, not proof of low risk.

principles.intro: The 19 mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. What must happen before anything else? Usually understanding objectives, finding the owner or analyzing the risk comes before any response. Containment comes first only in a declared incident.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what does everything else depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the most complete fit for your role: it brings risk within appetite, works on the cause and leaves the decision with the risk owner.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which would I defend to senior management?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST effective, MOST important or MOST appropriate. Judge the options on that quality only.
The core purpose or main reason, not a side benefit. A KRI exists to warn before the loss; a risk register exists to support decisions.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For risk or concern, the widest effect on business objectives, weighing likelihood and impact together, not technical severity alone.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and for which business objective?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What is most probable given the facts, even if another outcome would be worse.
Flip the logic. Three options do the job; find the one that helps or fits least. Rare on CRISC-style questions, so slow down when you see it.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is being asked: an action, a person, a document, a metric or a cause.

answering_routine.title: Find the priority word
answering_routine.text: Spot FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Check your role and the risk's stage
answering_routine.text: You are the risk practitioner unless told otherwise; owners decide. Is the risk identified, analyzed, treated, validated or reported? Note limiting facts such as “already”, “confirmed”, “within appetite” or “planned”.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options where you decide for the owner, act before analysis, mix up appetite and tolerance or a KRI and a KPI, or fix a symptom.

answering_routine.title: Decide between the final two
answering_routine.text: Apply the priority word, then prefer the next step not yet done, the one the other depends on, and the one that serves business objectives.

pace: 240 minutes for 150 questions is 96 seconds each. Aiming for about 90 leaves time to review flagged questions.
Checkpoints: around question 40 at 1 hour, 80 at 2 hours and 120 at 3 hours.
Past 2 minutes on one question, choose your best answer, flag it and move on. A wrong answer costs nothing extra, so never leave a blank.
Up to two breaks of 10 minutes or less, with the proctor's permission. The clock keeps running; a 90-second pace saves time for one short break.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as a fact or a priority word you missed the first time.
